body_markdown:
What if choosing a home meant choosing not just where you live, but how you want to live? Co-housing offers an alternative to traditional homeownership by combining private living spaces with shared amenities, meaningful relationships, and a stronger sense of community.


In this episode of[Home Green Homes](https://www.homegreenhomes.com/) , host Izumi Tanaka speaks with Hoa, a resident of[Corvidae Co-op](https://www.frolic.community/projects/corvidae-co-op) in South Seattle, about why her family chose co-housing and how the experience has shaped their daily lives. Watch the full conversation to learn more about life at Corvidae Co-op, the benefits and challenges of co-housing, and why this model could appeal to people looking for a more connected and sustainable future.


## More Than a Place to Live


For Hoa, the biggest motivation was the opportunity to build deeper relationships with her neighbors and create an intergenerational community where her young daughter could develop friendships with people of different ages. Rather than living in an isolated home, the family wanted a place where social connections could happen naturally.


At Corvidae Co-op, residents have their own private homes while sharing amenities such as community kitchens, laundry facilities, rooftop spaces, and a guest room. Regular community dinners and movie nights bring residents together, but some of the most meaningful moments happen spontaneously—like children knocking on a neighbor's door to play.


These everyday interactions illustrate one of co-housing's biggest benefits: connection is readily available without requiring every activity to be planned.


## Sustainability and Shared Living


Co-housing can also appeal to people who prioritize environmental responsibility. Corvidae Co-op was built with energy efficiency and future sustainability upgrades in mind. Its all-electric homes feature heat pumps and efficient appliances, while solar panels and electric vehicle charging were added after construction.


For residents, these features support a more sustainable lifestyle while helping manage household operating costs. The community also demonstrates how shared amenities and thoughtful design can support a different approach to residential living.


## Who Is Co-Housing Right For?


Although co-housing can benefit many people, it may be particularly appealing to families with children, environmentally conscious homeowners, singles, and older adults who value connection and community. It can offer opportunities for intergenerational relationships, informal social support, shared resources, and a greater sense of belonging.


However, community living also requires commitment. Residents may share responsibility for managing common spaces, organizing meals, maintaining the property, and working through disagreements. As Hoa explains, successful co-housing depends on communication, empathy, and a willingness to resolve conflict constructively.


Co-housing isn't for everyone, but for people who want closer relationships with their neighbors, it offers an alternative worth exploring.


## Rethinking What Makes a Home


Hoa's experience highlights an important idea: a sustainable home is about more than energy-efficient appliances, solar panels, or a smaller carbon footprint. It can also mean creating a healthier, more connected way of life.


By combining private homes with shared spaces and intentional community-building, co-housing challenges conventional ideas about homeownership and neighborhood design.


Corvidae Co-op was built in partnership with[Allied8 Architects](https://allied8.com/work-detail/corvidae/) , Green Canopy NODE, and[Frolic Community](https://www.frolic.community/who-we-are) , a mission-driven real estate developer building cooperative housing communities.
